definitions.explanation: Everything without exception. Has a somewhat old-fashioned or literary flavor, most commonly encountered in set phrases and compounds.

examples.japanese: {合切|がっさい}{捨|す}ててしまった。
examples.english: I threw away the whole lot.

examples.japanese: {荷物|にもつ}を{合切|がっさい}{袋|ぶくろ}に{入|い}れた。
examples.english: I put all my belongings into a drawstring bag.

examples.japanese: {何|なに}もかも{合切|がっさい}{引|ひ}き{受|う}けると{言|い}ってくれた。
examples.english: They said they would take on absolutely everything.

examples.japanese: {家財|かざい}{道具|どうぐ}を{合切|がっさい}{持|も}ち{出|だ}して{引|ひ}っ{越|こ}した。
examples.english: We moved out, taking every last piece of household furniture.

notes:
Composed of {合|がっ} (combine, bring together) and {切|さい} (all, entirely). The word means "everything gathered together" and has a slightly old-fashioned, literary quality. It is most commonly encountered in two forms.

The first is the standalone adverbial use meaning "everything, the whole lot," often paired with {何|なに}もかも for emphasis. The second is the compound {合切|がっさい}{袋|ぶくろ}, a traditional drawstring bag used to carry all of one's personal items — the name literally means "everything bag."

COMMON COLLOCATIONS:
- {合切|がっさい}{袋|ぶくろ}: drawstring bag for carrying everything (traditional)
- {何|なに}もかも{合切|がっさい}: absolutely everything
- {合切|がっさい}{捨|す}てる: to throw away the whole lot

SIMILAR WORDS:
- {一切|いっさい}: all, everything — more common in modern usage and applies to both affirmative and negative contexts ({一切|いっさい}ない = none at all)
- {全部|ぜんぶ}: all, everything — the everyday equivalent with no literary flavor
- {丸|まる}ごと: the whole thing, entirely — emphasizes wholeness rather than totality
